newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin op date "any day", says aide. [corrected 14:23 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin op date "any day", says aide. [corrected 14:23 gmt]

text.p: The date for Russian President Boris Yeltsin's heart operation could be set at any time, presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Friday.
Yastrzhembsky told a news conference that doctors were meeting every day and could decide at any time when to operate.
He said he sympathised with the view of Russian surgeon Renat Akchurin that there was no need to announce the date of the operation in advance, but he reassured reporters that this would not happen.
"The press will be told about the start of the operation, " he said.
(Corrects from "You will know about the date of the operation")
Akchurin, trained in Russia and in the United States, will lead the bypass operation, which will improve the flow of blood to Yeltsin's heart and enable him to resume a normal life.
Yeltsin virtually disappeared from public view between the two rounds of the Russian presidential election at the end of June. He finally announced on September 5 that he would have an operation.
He is currently in the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow while doctors carry out final tests.

U.S. specialist Michael DeBakey will advise Russian experts on the surgery, although Yastrzhembsky said foreign doctors would not be present in the operating theatre itself. He said DeBakey would arrive in Moscow on Saturday or Sunday.
DeBakey, who carried out the world's first successful heart bypass operation, told the Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper that Yeltsin was "in fine form".
"The operation can take place at any time, starting from next week. Doctors have successfully managed to cope with serious anaemia and a disfunctional thyroid gland," he said.
"I do not know the exact date of the operation yet. But I can say that Mr Yeltsin has been well prepared for it."
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had signed a decree giving Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin temporary authority to sign agreements with Russian regions.
Chernomyrdin will take over all Yeltsin's powers, including control of the button which could be used to launch a nuclear strike, during the operation itself.

Asked about rumours that the operation would be shown on television Yastrzhembsky said: "The operation itself and everything connected with it are not some sort of a show and there will naturally be no live transmission."
